title: Child-safety rules are common on paper, but systematic age assurance remains rare across online services
source_unit: OECD Age assurance practices of 50 online services used by children, service-level public-information benchmark
geography: 50 online services used by children; services operate across jurisdictions and the report compares publicly stated policies and practices rather than country populations

observations.period: Publicly available service information reviewed for OECD report published 25 June 2025

systematic_age_assurance_at_account_crea.unit: services systematically assuring age at account creation

any_age_assurance_mechanism.unit: services with some age-assurance mechanism, often triggered only in specific circumstances

no_systematic_account_creation_assurance.unit: services not systematically assuring age at account creation

systematic_share.unit: percent of benchmarked services systematically assuring age at account creation

observations.method: OECD review of publicly available age-related policies and practices for 50 online services used by children, with feedback sought from profiled services. The benchmark describes service design and stated practice, not observed user-level enforcement.
observations.uncertainty: Public information may omit internal controls, vary in detail, or change after publication. The benchmark does not test whether age assurance is accurate, privacy-preserving, accessible, effective against evasion, or consistently enforced across countries and products.
observations.subgroup: Online services used by children, their child and adolescent users, parents, regulators, service providers, and child-rights organisations.
observations.counterinterpretation: A service may use risk-based or feature-specific checks rather than universal account-creation assurance; universal checks can also create privacy, exclusion, bias, and access costs. The count therefore identifies implementation gaps, not a complete safety ranking.

observations.period: 2025 OECD benchmark of age-related policy and practice across the same 50 services

minimum_age_basis.value: often privacy or contract law rather than safety

geographic_variation.value: minimum ages can vary by geographic location

age_tiered_safeguards.unit: reported service-practice pattern; safeguards may be turned off or rely on parental controls

cross_border_implementation.unit: reported implementation condition for services operating across jurisdictions

observations.method: OECD qualitative comparison of terms, age thresholds, age-tiered safeguards, parental controls, triggering conditions, and jurisdictional variation in publicly available service information.
observations.uncertainty: Qualitative categories such as 'many' do not provide a complete service count in the public summary. A stated minimum age, parental control, or age tier is not proof that a child receives a safe or age-appropriate experience.
observations.subgroup: Children of different ages, parents and caregivers, services with different risk profiles, cross-border regulators, and online-safety and privacy institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Age assurance is only one control. Safety-by-design, reporting, moderation, data minimisation, education, parental support, and remedy channels may reduce risk even where age is not verified at sign-up; conversely, assurance can introduce new data and discrimination risks.

related_sources.claim: OECD companion analysis maps legal and policy variation in age assurance across OECD countries.
OECD child digital-wellbeing report supplies the adjacent exposure and well-being context.

boundary: This record adds a service-level implementation and cross-border governance route to the child-digital lane. It does not establish that any service is safe or unsafe, identify individual children, evaluate age-assurance accuracy, or resolve the privacy and inclusion trade-offs of stronger verification.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: OECD publication page and official report summary retrieved; 50-service denominator, 2 systematic account-creation checks, 26 services with some mechanism, and caveats on age tiers, parental controls, legal basis, and geography cross-checked against OECD materials.
